families.name: Federated Learning for Speech
families.definition: A distributed training paradigm where models are trained on local devices or silos without sharing raw data, aggregating only model updates to a central server.

properties.text: Preserves privacy by keeping raw speech data on local devices or within organizational silos.
Addresses non-IID data distributions through personalized models, adaptive averaging strategies, or client-adaptive training.
Reduces communication and computation costs using techniques like partial variable training, federated dropout, and lossy compression.
Can be combined with differential privacy guarantees to further protect individual user data.
Supports semi-supervised and incremental learning scenarios for production-scale systems.
Enables joint federated-centralized training to compensate for missing data domains in on-device caches.

limitations.text: Performance degrades significantly when data among clients is not independently and identically distributed (non-IID).
High communication and computation costs are associated with training large state-of-the-art models on edge devices.
Vulnerable to privacy attacks such as attribute inference and speaker information retrieval from model updates.
Requires careful handling of heterogeneous edge networks and limited device memory.
Lacks standardized benchmarks specifically for audio tasks until recent introductions like FedAudio.

families.name: Speech Anonymization and Privacy-Preserving Transformations
families.definition: Methods that transform speech signals to remove sensitive attributes such as speaker identity, gender, or emotion while preserving linguistic content.

properties.text: Uses content/speaker disentanglement and voice conversion to remove source speaker identity.
Employs generative adversarial networks (GANs) to synthesize voices that conceal gender or identity.
Applies adversarial reweighting or disentanglement to hide specific personal aspects like age, sex, or ethnicity.
Can generate utterance-specific perturbations to obscure sensitive words like digits in credit card numbers.
Utilizes secure multi-party computation or homomorphic encryption for privacy-preserving processing.
Aims to prevent attribute inference attacks by removing demographic traits from acoustic features.

limitations.text: There is no clear agreement on which privacy metrics to use, with different metrics exhibiting blind spots.
Transformations may degrade the utility of the speech for downstream tasks like recognition or emotion analysis.
Current methods often rely on pre-trained acoustic models that may themselves leak information.
Balancing the level of privacy achieved with the preservation of spoken content remains a challenge.
Some approaches require significant computational resources or complex cryptographic overhead.

families.name: Adversarial Attacks on Speech Systems
families.definition: Techniques that craft imperceptible or robust perturbations to speech inputs to cause misclassification, mistranscription, or misidentification in machine learning models.

properties.text: Includes targeted attacks that force specific malicious outputs and untargeted attacks that degrade performance.
Can be performed in white-box settings with full model access or black-box settings with only query access.
Utilizes psychoacoustic hiding to make perturbations imperceptible to humans.
Includes physical-world attacks that remain effective despite reverberation and noise from playback environments.
Targets various components including automatic speech recognition (ASR), speaker verification, and speech emotion recognition.
Can involve data poisoning, such as clean-label poisoning, to corrupt models during training.

limitations.text: Many attacks are not robust to physical-world conditions like background noise or reverberation.
Black-box attacks are more challenging and may have lower success rates than white-box attacks.
Adversarial examples can be detected by analyzing temporal dependencies or using transformation-based defenses.
Poisoning attacks require control over a fraction of the training data, which may be difficult to achieve in practice.
Attacks on speaker recognition systems are less studied in practical black-box settings compared to white-box scenarios.

families.name: Adversarial Defenses and Robustness
families.definition: Methods designed to detect, mitigate, or prevent the impact of adversarial perturbations on speech recognition and verification systems.

properties.text: Includes input transformation methods like mel domain noise flooding and cyclic GAN reconstruction.
Uses adversarial training to improve model robustness against known attack types.
Employs certified defenses like randomized smoothing to provide provable robustness guarantees.
Detects adversarial inputs by analyzing the consistency of transcriptions across different audio transformations.
Utilizes high-level representation guided denoisers to remove adversarial noise without amplifying errors.
Can be applied to both end-to-end ASR systems and modular pipelines.

limitations.text: Defenses may introduce a trade-off between robustness and clean-data accuracy.
Adversarial training can introduce disparities in performance across different demographic groups.
Certified defenses often provide loose guarantees or require significant computational overhead.
Many defenses are specific to certain attack types or threat models and may not generalize well.
Detecting adversarial examples in real-time with low latency remains a challenge.

families.name: Fairness and Bias Mitigation in Speech AI
families.definition: Approaches to identify, measure, and reduce performance disparities across demographic subgroups such as gender, race, and age in speech technologies.

properties.text: Identifies subgroups suffering from subpar performance using geographic and demographic information.
Applies adversarial reweighting to force models to focus on poorly performing instances.
Uses mixed-effects Poisson regression to control for confounding factors and interpret word error rate gaps.
Develops automated testing frameworks to simulate different environments and assess effectiveness for various populations.
Incorporates fairness constraints into model training objectives to learn fair representations.
Evaluates bias in speaker verification, ASR, and speech emotion recognition systems.

limitations.text: There is no clear agreement on which fairness definition to apply in each situation.
Fairness mitigation measures may reduce overall model accuracy.
Bias can arise from unrepresentative datasets, inadequate models, or human stereotypes in labeling.
Measuring fairness is complicated by unobserved heterogeneity across speakers.
Adversarial training for robustness can inadvertently introduce or exacerbate fairness disparities.

families.name: Privacy Attacks and Inference
families.definition: Methods that exploit vulnerabilities in speech models to infer sensitive information about training data or users, such as membership, speaker identity, or attributes.

properties.text: Includes membership inference attacks to determine if a specific data sample was used in training.
Performs attribute inference to predict sensitive traits like gender, age, or health status from acoustic models.
Extracts targeted training data from trained models using noise masking or fill-in-the-blank techniques.
Analyzes model updates in federated learning to retrieve speaker information.
Uses black-box access to evaluate the vulnerability of self-supervised and end-to-end models.
Can be used to audit whether a user has unwillingly contributed audio to a model.

limitations.text: Success of attacks depends on the specific model architecture and training data distribution.
Black-box attacks are more difficult to execute and may have lower precision and recall than white-box attacks.
Privacy-preserving techniques like differential privacy may not fully prevent all types of inference attacks.
Attacks on federated learning models require access to model updates, which may be restricted in some deployments.
There is a lack of comprehensive benchmarks for evaluating the privacy risks of speech models.

families.name: Self-Supervised and Large-Scale Speech Representation Learning
families.definition: Methods that learn general-purpose speech representations from large amounts of unlabeled audio data, which can be fine-tuned for downstream tasks.

properties.text: Pre-trains models on massive datasets of unlabeled speech to capture rich acoustic features.
Uses contrastive tasks or masked language modeling objectives to learn representations.
Achieves state-of-the-art performance on ASR and other tasks with minimal labeled data.
Generalizes well to standard benchmarks in zero-shot transfer settings.
Can be used for semi-supervised learning to improve performance with limited labeled data.
Enables the development of foundation models for robust speech processing.

limitations.text: Requires significant computational resources for pre-training.
May encode biases present in the pre-training data, such as gender or racial disparities.
Vulnerable to membership inference attacks due to memorization of training data.
Performance can vary across different demographic groups if the pre-training data is not representative.
Interpretability of the learned representations remains a challenge.
Developing standardized benchmarks for evaluating privacy, fairness, and robustness in speech AI systems.
Improving the efficiency of federated learning for large speech models on resource-constrained edge devices.
Designing privacy-preserving techniques that maintain high utility for downstream tasks like ASR and emotion recognition.
Mitigating the trade-off between adversarial robustness and fairness in speech models.
Creating effective defenses against black-box adversarial attacks in practical, real-world deployment scenarios.
Understanding and mitigating the privacy risks associated with self-supervised speech models, including memorization and membership inference.
Developing interpretable and fair speech representations that do not encode sensitive demographic attributes.
Standardizing the evaluation of speech anonymization techniques with metrics that balance privacy and utility.
Addressing the non-IID data challenge in federated learning to improve model convergence and performance.
Investigating the long-term societal and psychological impacts of speech AI errors and biases on marginalized groups.
